doc.title: Joe Ascione interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Future of the jazz party scene
summary: Jazz parties and festivals are waning, though new organizers appear, such as the Texas jazz society taking over a party.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: You think there’s a future for this jazz party thing?

You know I don’t have the answer to that yet but occasionally I think about it. For example I just saw Mat Domber’s son here in Clearwater. I think his name is Jeff, sorry Jeff if it’s not Jeff. And I see the sons and daughters of the people who run the jazz party scenes. And I always say I wonder if so-and-so is going to take over when so-and-so is not here. So on that side I think it’s very possible. And then I say okay, now a lot of people that I know have passed on, audience members, listeners. So in that sense it’s

waned quite a bit. Now I’ve never done one of those Dick Gibson parties. And I used hear like those things were major, tons of people, a slew of musicians, it was a real party. I mean we used to hear about the crazy — in a good way crazy, you know musically and socially. But so everybody’s always talking about those days and how it’s dried up in a sense that way. And it probably has. And that’s why they try to introduce it to young people and try to get them in and things like that. But the jury’s out on that as far as I’m concerned. I’m not sure how it’s going to go. It looks like it’s waning a little bit. But somehow things always creep up. Like this Texas — Odessa and Midland. It’s like the Hatfields and the McCoys always battling who’s going to do the jazz parties. Now the Jazz Society took it over. So see, something else came up. So I think it’s, again, cyclical. That’s the way — nothing’s static. It’s always in a state of change. You’ve just go to roll with it.
